question_type: geometric mean of 80 monthly budget-expenditure cells from a months-by-calendar-year summary table, where the question's year range ('just 1940-1949') pins which printings to use

opus_path.decision: Read the question as asking for a table of monthly budget expenditures laid out by calendar year whose rows are exactly 1940-1949. Counted 80 months (Mar 1942 to Oct 1948 inclusive) and used exp(mean ln x). Flagged two risks up front: basis changes between vintages and OCR errors in cells.

Listed the row years of 'Table 6.- Summary by Months and Calendar Years' in every 1948-1951 issue (scan.py). Only the Mar 1949 to Feb 1950 printings show exactly 1940-1949. Rejected Jan 1949 (old basis, rows 1939-1948) and Mar 1950 onward (wider year ranges, 1948 months re-based for the Foreign Economic Cooperation Trust Fund, and OCR year labels shifted by one).
Read the Budget expenditures block of the Feb 1950 printing, the last one with the 1940-1949 range and the first with a complete 1949 row.

Checked every row against its printed Total and took a per-cell majority across all 12 in-range printings (extract_all.py). This found two OCR-misread cells in Feb 1950 (May 1942, Nov 1947), which it corrected. Clean printings (Jun and Aug 1949) carry identical values, so the result does not depend on which in-range vintage is used.
calc.py first checks the identity expenditures = net receipts - surplus for every target month (the corrected cells pass), then takes the 80-value geometric mean and rounds it to 2 decimals.
An independent reviewer recomputed from the clean Jun 1949 printing, got the same result, and confirmed that only the Mar 1949 to Feb 1950 printings have exactly 1940-1949.

opus_key_moves: Used 'just the calendar years 1940-1949' to select the vintage: it listed each printing's row-year set and kept only printings whose table spans exactly that range, which excluded the re-based, label-shifted 1950-51 printings
Checked every extracted row against its printed Total and took a per-cell majority over 12 printings, which caught and repaired two OCR-misread cells
Cross-checked the repaired cells with an independent within-table identity (receipts - surplus = expenditures)

The benchmark likely uses raw values. We need match expected'; [73] 'Usually these tasks are generated from OCR text and expected answers computed from extracted table values, not human-corrected... we should use the corpus text as-is.'
first_divergence.consequence: Two understated cells pulled the geometric mean slightly low. The answer is off by well under 1%, but that is still wrong at 2 decimals.

Hand-typed 80-value lists into python -c and later credited a list containing a Jan 1950 OCR variant to the Dec 1949 printing. This bookkeeping error around printings did not affect the final choice.

adapter_context.notes: Base instructions only. They say nothing about OCR errors or about whether answers are keyed to printed values or OCR text.

remedies.intervention: State the answer convention explicitly: reference answers use the values printed in the original document. When a row's cells do not sum to its printed total, treat the offending cell as an OCR misread and repair it from other printings (majority) or from the total. Never answer from a cell you have shown to be misread.
remedies.why: The actor had already run the check in code and found the right digits. Its only reason for keeping the raw cells was a stated guess about how the key was built ([63], [73]), and a stated convention removes exactly that uncertainty.

remedies.intervention: Run a row-total validator automatically on every extracted table row (sum of cells vs printed Total, ±1-2 tolerance for rounding). It should return the suspect cell and a candidate correction from other printings.
remedies.why: It would have flagged the same two cells. But this actor already knew about them, so the check alone would not change its policy decision without the TEXT convention.

remedies.intervention: Add an 'all printings of this row' lookup that returns each cell's value in every issue carrying the row, plus the majority value.
remedies.why: Opus's deciding evidence was a 10-of-12 and an 11-of-12 majority (worklog.md:46-47). The actor spent about 25 steps collecting printings by hand.

secondary_errors.note: The three late printings disagree on the expenditure block's year labels because OCR dropped a row in different places. The arm trusted the one printing (Jan 1951) whose label sequence had no gap and declared Dec 1950 and Feb 1951 shifted, although those two agree with each other and with every 1949 printing. In Jan 1951 the labels are the ones that are off by one: its second-to-last year row is partial and its last year row is entirely blank (checked in the corpus at treasury_bulletin_1951_01.txt:400-419). So the arm read each year's months one calendar year late, which produced the 5-25% error.
Hand-typed the 80-value list and got 79. It fixed this by grouping values by year.

glm_expressed_doubt.where: At [33] it wrote 'Need anchor via annual totals or adjacent vintage' but then settled the question on label-sequence continuity alone. At [45] it noticed cell-level OCR differences in the Nov 1950 printing and did not revisit.

adapter_context.notes: The latest-vintage default was wrong here: the question pins the table by its row range, and the later printings were re-based. The arm followed it literally. The anchoring convention was right in spirit, and the arm paraphrased it at [33], but it anchored on label continuity instead of comparing row totals across adjacent vintages. The printings it dismissed outnumbered the one it trusted 2 to 1.

remedies.intervention: Add a cross-printing year-label check for tables with year rows. For each chosen row, compare its printed row Total with the same-labelled row in adjacent printings and flag a whole-row shift. Also flag a printing whose last labelled year is blank while the year before it is partial.
remedies.why: The arm had three late printings on screen and explicitly wanted to anchor via annual totals or an adjacent vintage [33], but used label continuity instead. An automatic comparison would have shown Jan 1951 as the odd one out: its row totals sit one label away from the other printings'.

remedies.intervention: Refine the vintage rule: when the question describes the table's own scope (e.g. 'for just the calendar years 1940-1949'), use printings whose table has exactly that scope. The latest-vintage default applies only when nothing in the question pins the table.
remedies.why: The arm followed the existing vintage text literally at [17] and [29], so an amended rule would likely be followed the same way.

remedies.intervention: Add a degenerate-repetition guard: when a reasoning block repeats the same sentence N times, force a short summary and a next action.
remedies.why: It would have saved time and tokens at [33], but the repetition was not the cause of the wrong answer.

right_arms_note: No arm was right. The none arm reached the same table, vintage and OCR diagnosis as Opus, then chose the raw OCR cells. The cards arm had a valid vintage but did no validation. The prompt arm followed the latest-vintage rule into re-based late printings with shifted year labels.
text_vs_mechanism: Mixed. For the none arm, a text convention ('answers use printed values; repair cells that fail their row totals') would plausibly have flipped a deliberate choice. The cards arm performed no check, and the prompt arm had vintage and anchoring text, followed it literally and still anchored on the wrong printing, so both need a mechanism: automatic row-total and cross-printing consistency checks.
notes: issue47 = true (the question's official answer or wording is disputed). Even so, the grade marks Opus right and all three GLM answers wrong, and Opus's reviewer named a raw-OCR-based key as the residual risk (review.md:15). OCR in this table family fails in two ways: digit misreads in individual cells (every in-range printing has some) and whole-row year-label shifts in the 1950-51 printings. Recurring pattern: the actor guesses how the benchmark key was generated ('raw OCR', 'generated from one table') and lets that override evidence it has already found (none arm [63], [73]). The same pattern decided Q60's prompt arm. Hand-typing 80-value lists into python -c is itself error-prone (prompt [36] miscounted; none [39] mixed printings). A tool that returns parsed rows as arrays with their source line would remove this.
